raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils, most often immunoglobulin light chain (AL) or transthyretin (ATTR) amyloid [1,2]. Although once considered rare, it is increasingly recognized because of heightened clinical awareness, scintigraphic diagnosis, and disease-modifying therapy [3-5]. AL amyloidosis arises from a clonal plasma-cell or B-cell disorder and is a hematologic emergency because circulating light chains can exert direct cardiotoxicity in addition to causing interstitial infiltration [3]. ATTR amyloidosis results from dissociation and misfolding of transthyretin tetramers; it may be hereditary/variant (ATTRv) or wild-type (ATTRwt), the latter predominating in older men and often presenting as heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation, conduction disease, or aortic-stenosis-like physiology [4,6-9].

Clinical suspicion is central. Red flags include unexplained left ventricular wall thickening, discordant low-voltage or pseudo-infarct electrocardiography, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, autonomic neuropathy, nephrotic proteinuria, macroglossia, periorbital purpura, persistent troponin elevation, and intolerance of standard heart-failure drugs [1,5,10]. Echocardiography typically shows concentric thickening, biatrial enlargement, restrictive filling, valve and interatrial septal thickening, pericardial effusion, and impaired longitudinal strain with relative apical sparing [11]. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) adds tissue characterization, with abnormal gadolinium kinetics, diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement, elevated native T1, and expanded extracellular volume; late gadolinium enhancement and extracellular volume also provide prognostic information [12,13].

Diagnosis must first exclude AL amyloidosis because treatment urgency and prognosis differ. Serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation are mandatory in all suspected cases [3,5]. When monoclonal testing is negative, grade 2 or 3 myocardial uptake on technetium-labeled bone scintigraphy, with appropriate single-photon emission computed tomography localization, can diagnose ATTR cardiomyopathy without biopsy [14,15]. If monoclonal proteins are present, scintigraphy is equivocal, or the phenotype is atypical, tissue confirmation with Congo red staining and amyloid typing—preferably mass spectrometry—is required [15,16]. Once ATTR is diagnosed, TTR sequencing distinguishes ATTRv from ATTRwt and enables cascade genetic counseling [16,17].

Prognosis is driven by cardiac involvement and stage. In AL amyloidosis, natriuretic peptides, troponins, and involved free light chains underpin staging and response assessment [18-20]. In ATTR, natriuretic peptides, troponin, renal function, functional class, and six-minute-walk distance help risk stratification; ATTRwt natural-history cohorts show progressive morbidity and mortality without disease-modifying treatment [8]. Atrial arrhythmias and intracardiac thrombus are common, and anticoagulation is generally favored for atrial fibrillation irrespective of conventional risk scores [30].

Management is multidisciplinary and combines supportive heart-failure care, arrhythmia management, and precursor-protein-directed therapy [16,17]. Loop diuretics are the foundation for congestion; mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists may help selected patients, whereas beta-blockers, renin–angiotensin inhibitors, and vasodilators are often poorly tolerated because stroke volume is fixed and autonomic dysfunction is common [16,17]. Pacemakers treat symptomatic bradyarrhythmias, but defibrillator decisions should be individualized because electromechanical dissociation may limit benefit [17].

AL therapy targets rapid and deep suppression of light-chain production. Consensus criteria define hematologic and cardiac responses and support early response-adapted escalation [20,21]. Daratumumab combined with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone has improved hematologic complete response and major organ deterioration-free survival and is now a key first-line regimen for eligible patients [22]. Autologous stem-cell transplantation remains an option for carefully selected low-risk patients, while advanced cardiac AL requires especially cautious dosing and close cardio-hematology coordination [3,21].

ATTR therapy has transformed the field. Tafamidis, a transthyretin kinetic stabilizer, reduced mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in ATTR cardiomyopathy [23]. Acoramidis, another stabilizer designed for high TTR stabilization, improved hierarchical clinical outcomes in ATTR cardiomyopathy [24,25]. Gene-silencing approaches reduce hepatic TTR production: patisiran and inotersen proved efficacy in hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy [26,27], and patisiran improved functional and health-status measures in ATTR cardiomyopathy [28]. Serial biomarkers and imaging, including CMR extracellular volume, may track disease regression or progression, particularly after effective AL therapy [29]. Future priorities include earlier detection in high-risk populations, comparative sequencing of stabilizers and silencers, combination therapy, and amyloid-depleting strategies.
